FACTS SUMMARY & MATRIMONIAL DISPUTE BACKGROUND:
Husband filed a petition for divorce under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act alleging adultery against his wife, and filed an interim application before the Family Court seeking a direction for their second minor child to undergo a DNA paternity test to establish the wife's alleged infidelity. The Family Court allowed the application, and the High Court affirmed the order.

Sub-Case Type: Divorce / Paternity & DNA Testing
Acts and Sections Invoked: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 [Sections: 13(1)(i)]; Indian Evidence Act, 1872 [Sections: 112, 114]; Family Courts Act, 1984; Constitution of India [Sections: 21]

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Section 112 of the Evidence Act establishes a conclusive presumption of legitimacy that can only be displaced by strong and cogent proof of non-access during conception. DNA testing touches upon the child's constitutional right to privacy, dignity, and legitimacy and cannot be ordered as a matter of course or as a shortcut to prove adultery. Refusal to submit a child to DNA testing does not invite adverse inference under Section 114(h) where access is admitted.

STATUTORY & JUDICIAL APPLICATION:
- Substantive relevance: Core matrimonial proceeding under Section 13(1)(i) HMA and Family Courts Act laying down governing principles for ordering DNA paternity tests in divorce proceedings.
- Decided by: V. RAMASUBRAMANIAN AND B.V. NAGARATHNA

Irretrievable breakdown of marriage is recognized as a valid factual ground for dissolution under Article 142, with parameters established regarding maintenance, alimony, child welfare, and duration of separation.

Under Section 12 HAMA, an adopted child is deemed to be the child of the adoptive parents only from the date of adoption; the old shastric doctrine of relation back does not apply post-1956. LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
The right to marry is a statutory and social institution governed by personal and statutory laws, not an unqualified fundamental right. Courts cannot rewrite the Special Marriage Act, 1954 because altering its gendered architecture would disrupt intertwined succession, maintenance, and divorce laws. Legislative action is necessary to recognize queer unions.

DECISION & ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT:
Writ petitions disposed of. The 5-Judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that there is no fundamental right to marry; unanimously held that the Special Marriage Act cannot be judicially re-written to include same-sex couples; by majority (3-2) held that unmarried queer couples cannot claim adoption under CARA guidelines without statutory amendment; recorded Union's undertaking to establish a committee to examine queer social rights.

LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED (RATIO DECIDENDI):
Under Section 15(1)(a) read with Section 16 (Rule 1) of HSA 1956, the heirs of a female Hindu dying intestate include the sons, daughters, and children of any pre-deceased son or daughter. By virtue of the branch representation rule, the widow of a pre-deceased son steps into her husband's shoes to inherit the share that would have fallen to the pre-deceased son.

A Hindu marriage is a sacrament and not a mere civil contract. Registration under Section 8 HMA is merely evidentiary and cannot cure the total absence of solemnization ceremonies.

Sub-Case: Constitutional Family Law / Restitution of Conjugal Rights (s.9 HMA) | Relevance: DIRECT
Acts and Sections: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 [Sections: 9, 13, 14]; Constitution of India [Sections: 14, 21]

FACTS:
Writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (Restitution of Conjugal Rights) on the ground that it violates the fundamental right to privacy, bodily autonomy, and equality under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.

ISSUES:
- Whether Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 providing for restitution of conjugal rights infringes the fundamental right to privacy and bodily autonomy under Article 21.
- Whether statutory restitution of conjugal rights is an unconstitutional state co-option of marital cohabitation.

HOLDING:
Writ petition heard and principles of constitutional scrutiny applied, upholding the statutory objective of marital reconciliation while emphasizing that courts cannot compel physical cohabitation through coercive execution.

RATIO DECIDENDI:
Section 9 of HMA is designed to encourage reconciliation and preservation of marriage, but a decree for restitution of conjugal rights cannot be executed by physical force or coercion against the will of a spouse, respecting constitutional privacy and dignity.

FACTS:
Reference on whether High Courts have inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC (or Section 528 BNSS) to quash complaints and proceedings initiated under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

ISSUES:
- Whether proceedings under Section 12 of the PWDVA are civil or quasi-criminal in nature.
- Whether High Courts can invoke inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash Section 12 PWDVA applications to prevent abuse of the process of court.
